title: Commitments
hookLine: sixth point: don't speak of others' faults, don't wait in ambush, don't be fickle

lines: A NAME COMES UP AT LUNCH.
cards: Somebody's name comes up at lunch. They aren't there. Within a minute the table has a verdict on them, and it isn't kind.
Nobody planned it; it just happens, the way water runs downhill. The old Tibetan mind-training teachings know that table well.
Their sixth point is a set of commitments, short lines to live by, and a few could have been written for that lunch. Don't talk about other people's faults. Don't wait in ambush.
Don't be fickle. Today, the promises that keep mind training honest.

teach.b: First, what a commitment is here. Tibetan tradition credits the seven points of mind training to the teacher Chekawa, who gathered teachings it traces back to Atisha.
The sixth point is a list of commitments: not laws handed down from above, but promises a student keeps so the practice doesn't quietly turn sour.

teach.h: OTHERS' FAULTS ARE EASY TO SEE.
teach.b: Second, don't speak of others' faults. The Dhammapada puts the problem plainly, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive."
Pointing out someone's weakness can feel like insight. Often it's a way of not looking at your own. Third, don't wait in ambush, your line today.

It means not storing up a hurt and keeping it ready for the right moment to pay someone back. A grudge can be very patient. The commitment asks you to put it down quietly, when nobody would ever know you had it.

Translators render it in different ways, but the sense is steadiness: not warm one day and cold the next. Kindness that depends on your mood hasn't been trained yet. Now the week: the preliminaries, first the basics.
Sending and taking, riding the breath. Trouble as the path. Five strengths.
Two witnesses. And today, commitments. One point is left, guidelines, and the seven are complete.
Notice where all of them aim: at your own mind, not at the person who isn't at the table.

how: Tibetan Buddhists who practice mind training (lojong) study the seven points with a teacher and often recite or reflect on their short lines, including the commitments of the sixth point, as reminders through the day.

o: strict vows a monk takes before a whole community
promises a student keeps so mind training stays honest
a pledge to sit in meditation for a set time each day

games.q: the sixth point: tap the pairs.
p: others' faults are easy to see
don't keep a hurt ready to pay back
not warm one day and cold the next

s: the commitments are laws handed down from above
they're promises a student keeps so mind training doesn't turn sour.
'don't wait in ambush' means don't store up a hurt to pay someone back
a grudge can be patient; the commitment asks you to put it down.
the Dhammapada says your own faults are the easy ones to see
it says the reverse: the fault of others is easily perceived, one's own is difficult to perceive.

games.q: a name comes up at lunch, someone who once hurt you. the table starts listing their faults, and you've got a good story to add. what does the sixth point ask?
o: tell it. it's true, after all.
keep it, and save it for a better moment.
let it go unspoken, and keep nothing in reserve.
games.why: two commitments meet here: don't speak of others' faults, and don't wait in ambush. no story now, and no grudge kept ready for later.

practice: Pick one of today's three, not speaking of a fault, not waiting in ambush, not blowing hot and cold, and bring to mind one person it touches: someone whose faults you could list without trying, or someone you've been quietly saving something for.
Hold them in mind and keep the promise: no case against them, no plan. If an old grievance rises, let it sit there, unused.

wordCard.voice: Commitments. The sixth point of mind training: promises a student keeps, like not speaking of others' faults and not waiting in ambush. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit samaya: a pledge or commitment. Tibetan teachers use the matching word, damtsik, for the commitments of mind training.

carryVoice: Your line: don't wait in ambush. Promises, not laws, kept for your own mind's sake. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive.

sources.ref: point six, the commitments of mind training
sources.work: The Seven Points of Mind Training (attributed to Chekawa Yeshe Dorje)
